summary: A one-line correction to RFC 107. On page 7 of that document a command shown as RTS should have been STR. Short errata notes like this were issued as RFCs in the early days.

eli5.summary: Someone found a typo in an earlier note and sent out a tiny memo saying which word was wrong and what it should be.

questions: what correction was made on page 7 of rfc 107
subtitle: A one-line 1971 correction: a command on page 7 of RFC 107 should be STR, not RTS.

tldr.problem: RFC 107 contained a mistake on its page 7.
tldr.mechanism: This memo states that the item shown as RTS (1.) should be an STR.
tldr.outcome: It is a complete erratum in a single sentence. Readers of RFC 107 should apply the fix.

today: RFC 124 updates RFC 107 with this correction, and its own status is listed as Unknown. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Correction
sections.content:
RFC 124, by J. Melvin of the NIC, is dated 19 April 1971. Its whole content is one sentence: on page 7 of RFC 107, the RTS (1.) should be an STR.

The header lists the category as C and says no RFCs are obsoleted. The memo does not explain what RTS or STR mean.
sections.eli5: A teacher says: on page 7, you wrote one word wrong, please swap it for this word.

sections.title: A Tiny Erratum as an RFC
sections.content: In 1971 even a single-line correction was issued as its own numbered RFC with its own NIC number (5840). The header text also names RFC 106 as the RFC updated, while the title and the unit metadata point to RFC 107; the correction itself concerns page 7 of RFC 107.
sections.eli5: Even a very small fix got its own numbered note, so everyone would see it.

sections.title: What to Take Away
sections.content: The change is purely a typo fix. It does not alter the design, and the text gives no further context. Anyone implementing the protocol from RFC 107 should read the RTS on page 7 as STR.
sections.eli5: Read the old page with the new word, and everything else stays the same.
